news.title: Democrats Might Expand Medicare if They Win the House. Lower Eligibility Age for Coverage Is on the Table.
news.text: House Democrats are developing an ambitious health care agenda that could go well beyond reversing President Donald Trump's policies if the party wins control of the U.S. House in November, with proposals ranging from expanding Medicare benefits to creating new government-run insurance options.According to a Washington Post report, Democrats involved in the discussions are considering lowering Medicare's eligibility age from 65, adding dental, vision and hearing benefits and limiting how much beneficiaries pay out of pocket each year. A public health insurance option and even coverage for children and young adults through age 26 are also being discussed.The proposals remain under discussion, and Democrats have not reached a consensus on many of the more expansive ideas. But the more immediate priorities like reversing Medicaid changes enacted under Trump's 2025 tax and spending law and restoring the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of last year have considerably broader support within the Democratic caucus.House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said this week there is "uniform Democratic support" for those two priorities, according to the Post. The stakes are significant, as the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated that Medicaid provisions in the 2025 reconciliation law will increase the number of Americans without health insurance by 7.5 million in 2034.CBO's latest projections show the total uninsured population rising from about 30 million in 2026 to 37 million by 2036, largely because of changes made by the law. Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Terri Sewell of Alabama are leading the House Democrats' Cost of Living Healthcare Working Group. The pairing brings together different wings of the party, with Ocasio-Cortez associated with the progressive caucus and Sewell with the centrist New Democrat Coalition."The first chance we get we're going to try to reverse the horrible cuts that the Trump administration has done," Sewell told the Post. Beyond those immediate changes, however, Democrats are examining policies that could significantly expand the federal government's role in health insurance.One option would lower the Medicare eligibility age, although lawmakers have not settled on a new threshold. Another would expand traditional Medicare to cover dental, vision and hearing services, benefits that have long been discussed by Democrats but remain largely outside standard Medicare coverage.Ocasio-Cortez told the outlet that reversing Medicaid changes would be the priority while arguing that Democrats should continue pursuing broader Medicare expansion. A government-run public option that would compete with private insurance plans is also under consideration, although Democrats currently lack agreement over how such a system would operate. Medicare-for-all remains part of the discussions as well.Other ideas range from improving long-term care benefits for seniors and expanding Medicare's ability to negotiate prescription drug prices to establishing government-backed health coverage for children through age 26. Democrats are also discussing changes to Medicare Advantage billing practices as one possible source of savings to help finance a larger package.
news.summary: The proposals remain under discussion, and Democrats have not reached a consensus on many of the more expansive ideas.
news.author: Matias Civita

news.title: Former Republican Governor and Trump Ally Jailed for Two Months
news.text: Former Kentucky Governor Matt Bevin was arrested Thursday after months of defying court orders in an ongoing family court and child support dispute, according to local media outlets. Bevin, a Republican and longtime ally of President Donald Trump who served as governor from 2015 to 2019, was taken into custody by the Bourbon County Sheriff’s Office and later booked into Louisville Metro Corrections. The arrest stems from an active bench warrant issued by Jefferson County Family Court Judge Angela Johnson after Bevin was found in civil contempt. The warrant, filed in June, requires Bevin to spend 60 days in jail and pay a $500 fine. Newsweek reached out to Bevin's lawyer via online form on Friday for comment. Arrested on a Movie Set According to local reports, the Bourbon County Sheriff’s Office acted on a tip that was called into 911. Deputies apprehended Bevin in Paris, Kentucky, where he was working as an extra on the set of The Greatest Christmas Gift. The owner of the property where the movie was being filmed, Jessica Mohr, told Louisville Public Media the sheriff arrived on set looking for Bevin. “The sheriff showed up and was asking some people if they’d seen his picture, and a young man was like, ‘I think that gentleman’s inside,’” Mohr recalled. “And then there he was, and he was sitting there speaking to the lead male actor, and yeah, he was arrested.” The legal battle centers on a dispute involving Bevin's ex-wife, Glenna Bevin, and their adopted son, Jonah. The court ordered both parents to submit comprehensive financial records—including tax returns and bank statements—as it weighs child support and financial provisions. While Glenna Bevin complied with the disclosures, Johnson ruled that the former governor repeatedly failed to turn over the mandatory documentation. A Contentious Family Dispute Jonah Bevin was one of four children Matt and his wife adopted from Ethiopia in 2012. Jonah alleged that his adoptive parents abandoned him at age 17 at a youth facility in Jamaica that was later shut down amid allegations of abusive conditions. After authorities intervened, Jonah said he was left to support himself and began seeking financial assistance, the Kentucky Lantern reported last year. Jonah responded to his father’s arrest by expressing sadness rather than celebration. In a statement released Friday to local outlet WLKY, Jonah said that “the sad reality is that adoption is supposed to be forever,” adding that his parents’ actions had made clear to him that they had not felt that kind of love for him “in a long time.” His attorneys, John Helmers Jr. and Melina Hettiaratchi, emphasized to the local station that the arrest was not something Jonah wanted, saying there was “no cause for celebration” when enforcing a parent’s obligations requires an arrest. They said Jonah had sought only the basic financial support he needed to rebuild his life and expressed hope that the court’s action would lead to accountability. Judge’s Sharp Rebuke The dispute has been ongoing for months. Bevin was previously held in contempt in May after failing to appear in court and avoided jail time by paying a $250 fine, the Kentucky Lantern reported. The former governor said he missed the court hearing because a boulder crashed into a home he owns in Maine. The judge subsequently ordered him to produce the records by June 5. Shortly before the deadline, Bevin’s attorney requested additional time to provide the remaining financial records, but Johnson denied the request and issued an arrest warrant, the outlet reported. Johnson criticized Bevin on Friday for what she characterized as his continued failure to cooperate with the court, according to Louisville Public Media. “You have done nothing to show the court that you are willing to act in good faith, and I cannot reward that with a reduced sentence or an alternative sentence or some form of relief for you.” “I will not allow you to taint the integrity of this court or any court with that kind of behavior,” Johnson added. The immediate focus now will likely be on whether Bevin provides the requested financial records and is potentially released or remains in custody while serving the 60-day sentence. Trump and Bevin's History Explained During his single term as governor, Bevin was a prominent conservative figure and a vocal ally of Trump. Trump strongly backed Bevin’s 2019 reelection campaign, giving him his “Complete and Total Endorsement” and holding a rally in Lexington on the eve of the election. Bevin, in turn, aligned himself closely with the president and his agenda, making the president’s support a part of his reelection effort. Bevin ultimately lost to Democrat Andy Beshear by roughly 5,000 votes. At the time, the Associated Press described Bevin as a “close ally” of Trump. Newsweek also reached out to the White House via email for comment. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jason Lemon and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: The arrest stems from an active bench warrant issued after former Kentucky Governor Matt Bevin was found in civil contempt.

news.title: Trump Adviser Peter Navarro Confirms Maria Bartiromo Sent Him Internal Fox Guidance
news.text:
Peter Navarro, a senior adviser to Donald Trump, confirmed Friday that Maria Bartiromo sent him internal Fox Business Network guidance about coverage of the president’s 2020 election claims, providing on-the-record support for a key detail in reports surrounding her abrupt departure from Fox News Media.

Navarro, Trump’s senior counselor for trade and manufacturing and a longtime adviser to the president, told Puck that Bartiromo texted him a screenshot of the guidance after he had been scheduled to appear on “Mornings With Maria” to discuss voter fraud.

According to Puck, Ralph Giordano, Fox Business senior vice president of programming, sent the guidance to Bartiromo’s producers ahead of Trump’s July 16 primetime speech about election integrity. The guidance directed the show not to pursue coverage of Trump’s claims involving China and the 2020 election.

Navarro told the outlet that Bartiromo sent him the screenshot and indicated that Fox executives did not want her discussing the subject on air. Puck reported that Navarro had been booked on the show to discuss voter fraud before the segment was scrapped.

Puck highlighted that Bartiromo may argue that she was simply alerting Navarro, a scheduled guest, to a change in the show’s lineup rather than improperly sharing confidential information.

Representatives for the White House, Bartiromo and Fox News did not immediately respond to TheWrap’s request for comment.

Navarro’s confirmation added a named source to the still-disputed account surrounding Bartiromo’s exit. TheWrap reported Thursday that multiple reports, citing sources familiar with the matter, said Bartiromo shared internal Fox guidance outside the company. Those reports linked the disclosure to her departure, though Fox has not publicly said why it parted ways with Bartiromo.

Fox News Media announced Thursday that Bartiromo was “no longer with FOX News Media,” effective immediately, ending her more than 12-year run at the company. Fox did not provide a specific reason for the decision and subsequently told TheWrap that her departure was a “business decision.”

Bartiromo’s attorney Bryan Freedman pushed back Friday on reports surrounding her exit, telling TheWrap that claims she was fired or was no longer a Fox employee were “absolutely and unequivocally false.”

“The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false,” Freedman said. “Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise.”
news.summary:
The president's senior counselor for trade and manufacturing shares he received a text message from the now-ousted Fox News personality

news.title: Trump says 'nobody will' build monuments for him after he's gone
news.text:
In a candid interview, President Donald Trump admitted that the various construction projects he has undertaken in Washington, DC, are an effort to build monuments to himself, saying, “Nobody will do it once I’m gone.”

Trump’s comments to New York Magazine came as the outlet asked the president about monuments such as the “triumphal arch” in the nation's capital.

“Nobody will do it once I’m gone. When I leave here, nobody will,” Trump said.

The “triumphal arch” is only one of many projects Trump has begun construction of in Washington, DC, with the deeply controversial White House ballroom being another of the president's marquee construction projects.

Despite the controversy, Trump said “the people should be thankful” for the ballroom.

“A lot of people said, ‘Don’t do this interview.’ But I’m proud of the work I’m doing,” Trump added.

Trump constructing his legacy

Construction of Trump’s $400 million White House ballroom, which has faced a slew of legal challenges since its start, got a major boost Aug. 31 as the Supreme Court cleared the way to continue construction.

Acting on an emergency appeal from Trump's administration, the court ruled 5-4 that a federal judge wrongly paused the project until a legal fight could be resolved.

In an unsigned opinion, a majority of the justices said the administration is likely to win its argument that the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the plaintiff in the pending lawsuit, cannot show sufficient, direct harm.

Trump has also sought to add his name to The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

Last month, the Kennedy Center's board again voted to put Trump's name on the building and rename its grounds the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.” However, the move remains tied up in court and has not taken effect.

The board's decision came despite a federal judge previously ruling that the center's official name cannot be changed without Congress. Government lawyers argue the new signage would recognize Trump's role in renovating the building rather than formally renaming it.

Falklands War hero Simon Weston dismisses Javier Milei's 'ridiculous' threat to retake the islands

By MARK NICOL, DEFENCE EDITOR

Published: 23:22 BST, 4 September 2026 | Updated: 23:35 BST, 4 September 2026

Britain's most celebrated Falklands War veteran has dismissed Argentine threats to retake the islands as 'ridiculous'.

Welsh Guardsman Simon Weston, who suffered severe burns in the 1982 South Atlantic conflict, said Argentina's latest claims to the British territory 'mean absolutely nothing'.

Mr Weston survived the sinking of the Royal Navy ship Sir Galahad after it was struck by a missile. Of his platoon of 30 men, 22 were killed.

But the veteran rubbished prospects that Argentina could retake the islands.

'The Argentine navy is mainly where we left it, at the bottom of the sea,' he told the BBC. 'They haven't invested in their army. They've bought some jets from Denmark but I don't think they are going to use force. 

'(Argentine president Javier) Milei has said they're not going to fight but he could change his position overnight.'

Mr Weston added that Donald Trump, who has appeared sympathetic to Mr Milei's position, was 'throwing a hissy fit', after Britain declined to support the US campaign against Iran.

He also hit back at Mr Milei, who said that 'winds of change' favoured his country's claim to the islands.

Welsh Guardsman Simon Weston, who suffered severe burns in the 1982 South Atlantic conflict, said Argentina's latest claims to the British territory 'mean absolutely nothing'

Military experts agree that Argentina could not recover the Falklands by force due to the presence of a British military garrison on the islands, including a quartet of RAF Typhoon jets

Argentine president Javier Milei has insisted he will 'act swiftly' to 'recover' the Falkland Islands, which he claims belong to Argentina by law and historical precedent

'They're just empty words and they mean absolutely nothing. It is just rhetoric – he's sabre-rattling again, unsettling the Islanders, but playing to the crowd.

'Argentina is in economic crisis – that's what caused them to invade 44 years ago. Nothing has changed.'

Mr Weston said the Argentine president's proposed sanctions on oil companies were 'ridiculous' because the firms 'haven't got a footprint' in their country.

Military experts agree that Argentina could not recover the Falklands by force due to the presence of a British military garrison on the islands, including a quartet of RAF Typhoon jets.

The closest Argentine airfields are 300 nautical miles from the islands, while its air and naval forces do not include sufficient refuelling assets to sustain attacks by the recently purchased F-16s.

Six of the US-manufactured but previously Danish-owned jets arrived in Argentina in November last year. 

A further 18 are expected by 2028. It is understood the UK did not oppose the sale.

The Typhoons from the RAF's 1435 Flight comprise a quick-reaction force should Argentina launch any attack. The Sky Sabre air defence system positioned on Mount Byron also provides protection.

Former Royal Navy commander Tom Sharpe said: 'Could Argentina invade us tomorrow? The answer is no. They lack the logistic support. 

'In 1982 they had the famous aircraft carrier the General Belgrano. They don't today. Back then the military junta ruling the country calculated a rapid operation might create a fait accompli before Britain could respond effectively.

'It was a gamble that didn't pay off. I don't think they'd try that again.'

Some 255 British servicemen were killed in the 1982 conflict.

news.title: Trump Signs Order Allowing Ranchers to Process Their Own Meat, Sell It Across State Lines
news.text:
President Donald Trump signed two executive orders on Friday to empower American ranchers, one of which allows them to process their own meat and sell it to consumers across state lines.

Trump signed the order, and another authorizing ranchers to protect against Mexican gray wolves, while flanked by ranchers and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins.

“Today, I’m thrilled to announce that my administration is taking historic action to help our nation’s great cattle ranchers and deliver American meat processed to the highest standard … there will be no standard higher in the world, and sold at the lowest prices directly to the consumer,” the president said.

“So for the first time ever, we’re going to give farmers and ranchers the right to process their own food. That’s a big announcement,” he went on to add. 

Trump said he will establish a program through which ranchers can bypass the four major companies that hold what he called “a monopoly” on processing the food. Trump assured that “very strong safety inspections” will be conducted on the meat.

According to the White House, under the order, Rollins is directed to take a number of actions within the Department of Agriculture:

The Order directs the Secretary of Agriculture to prioritize investigations into potential violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act, increase federal resources for these investigations, and review existing policies under the Act to strengthen protections for producers and ensure effective deterrence.
The Order directs the Secretary of Agriculture to modernize meat inspections to focus on core safety, boost processing efficiency and technology, lower costs to add value for ranchers and consumers, and remove unnecessary and burdensome requirements that do not support essential food safety needs.
The Order directs the Secretary of Agriculture to create a “one stop shop” resource and coordinator position within the Department of Agriculture to expand federal licensing and connect producers to inspection options, provide additional resources and training for small and very small meat processors, expand interstate market access for eligible meat products, and streamline processes to increase State participation in the State Meat and Poultry Inspection Program, the Cooperative Interstate Shipment Program, and the Talmadge-Aiken Cooperative Inspection Program.
The Order directs the Secretary of Agriculture to establish a “Strengthening Processing for U.S. Ranchers” loan program to help small and regional processors continue their operations, expand their footprint, and increase diversity of animal proteins being processed.

The second order directs a review and modernization of all federal “agency regulations and policy to promote ranchers’ interests,” including a review of whether gray wolves can be delisted or downlisted as an endangered species.
